title: Why square integrability?
text: Explain why the set of square-integrable functions is suitable for representing wave functions.
answer:
1.
A position wave function must have finite $\int|\psi(x)|^2dx$ so a nonzero state can be normalized to total probability 1.
2.

Square-integrable functions, identifying functions equal except on sets of zero length, form a vector space.
Its inner product is $\langle\phi|\psi\rangle=\int\phi^*(x)\psi(x)dx$; the Schwarz inequality ensures it is finite.
3.

This space $L^2$ is complete under its induced norm, so it is a Hilbert space.
Thus superpositions and norm limits remain valid state vectors.
Idealized plane waves are generalized states rather than normalizable members of $L^2$.

title: Normalize an exponential
text: Show that the function ψ(x) = A e⁻ᵃ|ˣ|, a > 0, is square-integrable. Find the normalization constant A.
answer:
1. Taking the absolute-value square gives $|\psi(x)|^2=|A|^2e^{-2a|x|}$.

2. The integrand is even, so $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\psi(x)|^2\,dx=2|A|^2\int_0^{\infty}e^{-2ax}\,dx$.

3. For $a>0$, $\int_0^\infty e^{-2ax}\,dx=\left[-e^{-2ax}/(2a)\right]_0^\infty=1/(2a)$. Thus the squared norm is $|A|^2/a<\infty$ for finite $A$, proving square-integrability.

4. Normalization requires $|A|^2/a=1$. Hence $|A|=\sqrt a$; choosing real positive $A$ gives $A=\sqrt a$. More generally $A=\sqrt a\,e^{i\theta}$, since a global phase does not change probabilities.

title: Prove Schwarz inequality
answer:
1. If $|\phi\rangle=0$, both sides are zero, so the Schwarz inequality holds with equality. Otherwise $N=\langle\phi|\phi\rangle>0$.

2. Put $s=\langle\phi|\psi\rangle$, $c=s/N$, and $|r\rangle=|\psi\rangle-c|\phi\rangle$. This choice makes $\langle\phi|r\rangle=s-cN=0$.

3. Positive definiteness gives $0\le\langle r|r\rangle=\langle\psi|\psi\rangle-c\langle\psi|\phi\rangle-c^*\langle\phi|\psi\rangle+|c|^2N=\langle\psi|\psi\rangle-|s|^2/N$. Multiplying by $N>0$ yields $|\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^2\le\langle\phi|\phi\rangle\langle\psi|\psi\rangle$.

4. Equality occurs exactly when $r=0$, meaning the nonzero vectors are linearly dependent. Zero-vector cases also give equality.

title: When is AB Hermitian?
text: Show that if Â and B̂ are Hermitian, then ÂB̂ is Hermitian only if Â and B̂ commute.
answer:
1.
For finite matrices, $(AB)^\dagger=B^\dagger A^\dagger$.

2.
Because $A$ and $B$ are Hermitian, $(AB)^\dagger=BA$.

3.
Therefore $AB$ is Hermitian exactly when $AB=(AB)^\dagger=BA$, or $[A,B]=0$.
For unbounded operators, product domains require additional care.

title: General uncertainty bound
text: Derive the general uncertainty relation ΔÂ ΔB̂ ≥ ½ |⟨[Â, B̂]⟩|.
answer:
1. For normalized $|\psi\rangle$, let $A'=A-\langle A\rangle I$, $B'=B-\langle B\rangle I$, $|\alpha\rangle=A'|\psi\rangle$, and $|\beta\rangle=B'|\psi\rangle$. Here $\langle A\rangle=\langle\psi|A|\psi\rangle$. Hermiticity gives $\langle\alpha|\alpha\rangle=\langle A^2\rangle-\langle A\rangle^2=(\Delta A)^2$, and similarly for $B$. Assume finite variances and the necessary operator domains.

2. Schwarz gives $(\Delta A)^2(\Delta B)^2\ge|z|^2$, where $z=\langle\alpha|\beta\rangle=\langle A'B'\rangle$.

3. Since $z^*=\langle B'A'\rangle$, $z-z^*=\langle[A,B]\rangle$. Thus $\operatorname{Im}z=\langle[A,B]\rangle/(2i)$ and $|z|^2=(\operatorname{Re}z)^2+(\operatorname{Im}z)^2\ge\tfrac14|\langle[A,B]\rangle|^2$.

4. Taking nonnegative square roots yields $\Delta A\,\Delta B\ge\tfrac12|\langle[A,B]\rangle|$.

title: Real eigenvalues
text: Prove that the eigenvalues of a Hermitian operator are real.
answer:
1. Let $A|v\rangle=\lambda|v\rangle$ with $v\ne0$. Taking the inner product with $v$ gives $\langle v|Av\rangle=\lambda\langle v|v\rangle$.

2. Hermiticity gives $\langle v|Av\rangle=\langle Av|v\rangle=\lambda^*\langle v|v\rangle$, because the first inner-product slot conjugates its scalar coefficient.

3. Therefore $(\lambda-\lambda^*)\langle v|v\rangle=0$. The nonzero eigenvector has strictly positive squared norm, so it can be cancelled and $\lambda=\lambda^*$.

4. A complex number equal to its complex conjugate has zero imaginary part. Hence every eigenvalue of the Hermitian operator is real.

title: Orthogonal eigenvectors
text: Prove that eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues of a Hermitian operator are orthogonal.
answer:
1.
Let $A|u\rangle=a|u\rangle$ and $A|v\rangle=b|v\rangle$, with distinct real $a,b$.

3.
Therefore $(b-a)\langle u|v\rangle=0$.
Since $a\ne  b$, $\langle u|v\rangle=0$, which proves orthogonality.

title: Changing a basis
text: Show how an operator transforms under a change of basis.
answer:
1. Let $\{|i\rangle\}$ and $\{|e_j\rangle\}$ be the old and new orthonormal bases. Define $U_{ij}=\langle i|e_j\rangle$, so $|e_j\rangle=\sum_iU_{ij}|i\rangle$. Orthonormality gives $(U^\dagger U)_{mn}=\sum_iU_{im}^*U_{in}=\delta_{mn}$, so $U$ is unitary.

2. Expand both basis vectors: $A'_{mn}=\langle e_m|A|e_n\rangle=\sum_{ij}U_{im}^*\langle i|A|j\rangle U_{jn}=\sum_{ij}U_{im}^*A_{ij}U_{jn}$. Therefore $A'=U^\dagger AU$, and state coordinates satisfy $c'=U^\dagger c$.

3. For a general invertible change-of-basis matrix $S$, whose columns need not be orthonormal, use $A'=S^{-1}AS$ and $c'=S^{-1}c$.

title: Fourier transform & probability
text: Explain how the position-space and momentum-space wave functions are related by a Fourier transform. Write the integral transformation from ψ(x) to ϕ(p). Explain the physical meaning of |ψ(x)|² and |ϕ(p)|².
answer:
1. Choose $\langle x|p\rangle=(2\pi\hbar)^{-1/2}e^{ipx/\hbar}$. Inserting the position completeness relation into $\phi(p)=\langle p|\psi\rangle$ gives $\phi(p)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\langle p|x\rangle\langle x|\psi\rangle\,dx$.

2. Conjugate symmetry gives $\langle p|x\rangle=(2\pi\hbar)^{-1/2}e^{-ipx/\hbar}$, hence $\phi(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-1/2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-ipx/\hbar}\psi(x)\,dx$. Conversely $\psi(x)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-1/2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{ipx/\hbar}\phi(p)\,dp$.

3. $|\psi(x)|^2$ and $|\phi(p)|^2$ are position and momentum probability densities. For an interval $[a,b]$, the position probability is $\int_a^b|\psi(x)|^2\,dx$; momentum probabilities are analogous. For a normalized state the full integrals of both densities equal 1.

title: A 2 × 2 Hermitian operator
text:
In a two-dimensional Hilbert space spanned by the orthonormal basis {|1⟩, |2⟩} an operator Â acts on the basis vectors as follows:
Â|1⟩ = 2|1⟩ + i|2⟩ and Â|1⟩ = −i|1⟩ + 3|2⟩
• Construct the 2 × 2 matrix representation of Â.
• Determine whether Â is Hermitian.
• Find the eigenvalues of Â.
answer:
1. The PDF gives two different outputs for $A|1\rangle$, so taken literally no linear operator satisfies both equations. The following complete calculation is conditional on the intended second input being $|2\rangle$.

2. The basis outputs give columns $\begin{pmatrix}2\\i\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}-i\\3\end{pmatrix}$, so $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&-i\\i&3\end{pmatrix}$.

3. Its Hermitian adjoint is $A^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}2&-i\\i&3\end{pmatrix}=A$. Therefore the corrected matrix is Hermitian.

4. The secular equation is $\det(A-\lambda I)=(2-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-(-i)(i)=\lambda^2-5\lambda+5=0$.

5. The quadratic formula gives $\lambda_\pm=(5\pm\sqrt5)/2$. Their sum is 5 and product is 5, agreeing with the trace and determinant.

title: Derive the Fourier pair
text: Given a state vector |ψ⟩, its position-space wavefunction is ψ(x) = ⟨x|ψ⟩ and its momentum-space wavefunction is ϕ(p) = ⟨p|ψ⟩. Using the continuous completeness relation, show that ψ(x) and ϕ(p) form a Fourier transform pair.
answer:
1. insert the position completeness relation: $\phi(p)=\langle p|I|\psi\rangle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\langle p|x\rangle\langle x|\psi\rangle dx$.

2.
Use $\langle p|x\rangle=(2\pi\hbar)^{-1/2}e^{-ipx/\hbar}$ to obtain $\phi(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-1/2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-ipx/\hbar}\psi(x)dx$.

3.
Conversely, insert $I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|p\rangle\langle p|dp$ into $\psi(x)=\langle x|I|\psi\rangle$ to get $\psi(x)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-1/2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{ipx/\hbar}\phi(p)dp$.
These are the forward and inverse Fourier transforms.
